title: Extend the messaging schema: reactions and blocks
problem: The messenger gets two features: emoji reactions on messages, and blocking users. Design both tables in schema_ext.py so the database itself rejects every invalid row, and make open_db() turn on foreign key enforcement. The tests only insert and delete rows and check what the database accepts.
requirements: reactions has the columns message_id, user_id, emoji, created_at; blocks has blocker_id, blocked_id, created_at
A reaction must point to an existing message and an existing user; a block to two existing users
The same user can't add the same emoji to the same message twice; different emoji, users or messages are fine
emoji and created_at are required; emoji can't be the empty string
Deleting a message deletes its reactions
No one can block themselves; a block exists at most once per (blocker, blocked) pair, and the direction matters
open_db() enforces foreign keys on its connection
contract: EXTRA_SCHEMA: str with two CREATE TABLE statements, run after chatdb.SCHEMA and chatdb.DATA. open_db() -> sqlite3.Connection with PRAGMA foreign_keys returning (1,)
expectedBehavior: Inserting reaction (1, 2, '👍', ...) works; inserting it again raises sqlite3.IntegrityError; DELETE FROM messages WHERE id = 1 removes that message's reactions; inserting block (3, 3, ...) raises sqlite3.IntegrityError
edgeCases: Same user, same message, different emoji: allowed
Unknown message id or user id: rejected
A blocks B and B blocks A: both allowed
Foreign keys only work if the connection turns them on
hints: Conceptual: every rule in the docstring is one constraint. 'Points to an existing row' is a foreign key, 'at most once per combination' is a primary key or UNIQUE over several columns, 'can't be X' is NOT NULL or CHECK, 'disappears with' is an ON DELETE action.

Specific: neither table needs its own id column; a composite PRIMARY KEY over (message_id, user_id, emoji) and over (blocker_id, blocked_id) expresses 'only once'. A table-level CHECK can compare two columns. SQLite ignores foreign keys unless the connection runs PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON.

Implementation: message_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES messages(id) ON DELETE CASCADE; emoji TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (emoji <> ''); PRIMARY KEY (...) and CHECK (blocker_id <> blocked_id) go after the columns. In open_db, run the PRAGMA before executescript.
evaluation: Every rule is enforced by the schema, not by Python code
Each table has a primary key that matches its 'only once' rule
ON DELETE CASCADE only where the docstring asks for it
